item.title: Why Teaching Consent Isn't Enough to End Sexual Violence
item.description:
Sexual Abuse

Why Teaching Consent Isn't Enough to End Sexual Violence

Consent education matters, but it can't address entitlement, status, and silence.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Sexual behavior can be a way to establish status, and that has dangerous ramifications.
  • Individual accountability isn’t enough to stop sexual violence; there’s much that allows it to continue.
  • Institutions frequently protect perpetrators rather than sexual violence survivors.
Sexual violence does not occur in a vacuum. The cultures and institutions surrounding it matter.
Source: Vadim Sherbakov / Unsplash

As a sex therapist and an educator, I keep thinking about what the “Cornell 7” case is illuminating. A brief overview: A woman, publicly identified as Jane Doe, has sued Cornell and seven male students, accusing them of drugging and raping her in October 2024.1 Details of the case are still emerging, and I can’t speak to what happened because I wasn’t there, but what I can say with confidence is that we cannot meaningfully address sexual violence only by teaching people to identify consent at the point of sexual contact.

Over the last few years, consent has rightfully taken a more prominent place in society. We emphasize it in conversations, seminars, and the law. If someone says “no” to sexual activity, it’s a no, and they haven’t consented. But we also have to look at what people learn long before the moment of sexual contact. How do they understand another person's desire? And it’s important to understand that a sexual assault should not be understood through the same framework as mutual desire because it involves a violation of another’s autonomy as well as consent. We have to ask: What do those who commit sexual assault believe they are entitled to? What happens when sexual behavior becomes a way of establishing status with other men?

We see the status aspect play out in numerous ways — men bragging about their “body count,” i.e., the number of women they’ve slept with, how they rank women based on attractiveness, and how they talk about women amongst themselves. For instance, a message in the Snapchat group chat from the Cornell case suggested that Jane Doe was available for sex. A later message asked if the "shop" was still open, and someone replied, "Yea," as though she was an object for the taking.

It’s disgusting and vile, but is anyone actually surprised? I know I’m not, and many of the women and people from historically marginalized communities I am talking with aren’t either. They are angry and tired. Some are disgusted. But there is a familiarity to this case that is hard to ignore.

Teaching about consent is not enough. And individual accountability isn’t either. If we stop at the individual, we miss too much because that doesn’t ask, “What allows this to continue?” What allows it to continue is cultural and systemic. There is a long history of cisgender men finding protection within systems built largely by and for other cisgender men. Research confirms this. A 2024 review article found that institutional betrayal, or causing further harm to survivors of college sexual violence, is rampant.2 Protecting cisgender men does not always require someone consciously deciding to protect another man. Sometimes the system does the work. People follow procedure but the procedure favors the perpetrator over the survivor.2

Or, it could be that the people at a university seek to protect the institution's reputation. I’ve known this for decades, and when I was in college, I cofounded a group called Sexual Assault and Violence Ends (S.A.V.E). This was necessary on that college campus to help raise awareness about sexual assaults that get brushed under the rug by institutions, and to create a safe space for students to seek support.

Sometimes protecting cisgender men means remaining loyal to their friend, or deciding what’s occurring is none of their business. Eventually, responsibility becomes so dispersed that everyone can tell themselves it belongs somewhere else, and that’s what allows sexual violence to fester.

To take a case that is not disputed, look at Jeffrey Epstein. The abuse itself is no longer a mystery.3 Neither is the fact that Epstein moved among people with extraordinary wealth and power for years. What remains difficult to comprehend is how sexual exploitation could continue for so long with so many people and institutions around him. I am less interested in treating that as the story of one exceptionally predatory man than in asking what made his continued access possible.

Systems do not always protect people equally. Survivors of sexual violence know something about this. Women do too. Black people have their own history with institutions in this country, as do queer and trans people. I’m not sharing new information – this is all widely known – but what I am saying is that until we stop treating sexual violence as only an individual problem, it will likely continue.

item.title: Attuning to the Collective Nervous System
item.description:
Trauma

Attuning to the Collective Nervous System

Our bodies are wired for regulation — can we accomplish this together?

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • In envisioning the collective nervous system, a tendency might be to look outside.
  • Instead, practice what it feels like to look through eyes from within the collective.
  • As our digital connectivity brings us closer as humans, so should our nervous systems.
  • A pathway for social change is moving from traumatized to trauma-integrative.

How the human nervous system organizes our bodies is nothing short of miraculous. When regulated, the systems of our body work in cooperation, ensuring homeostasis. In a state of hyperarousal or dysregulation, many physiological processes become activated, usually set off by stress.

Researchers continue to unpack new discoveries about the individual nervous system. As co-authors, we are curious about what it might mean to investigate a "collective nervous system." This question connects to the field of collective intelligence, which examines how networks of cooperative behavior solve problems at the level of cells, tissues, and whole organisms. We do not claim quantifiable proof of a collective nervous system. Instead, we invite you to work with the concept as a practice: to explore it through your own experience, with curiosity, and in conversation with others, and to notice what the potential is for individual and collective healing.

Looking Through Our Collective Nervous System

In envisioning the collective nervous system, our tendency might be to look outside, visualizing a group of individuals who are wired together through their central nervous systems. But what if we explored what it feels like from within the collective? What’s the subtlest form of awareness we can access? How and what does the collective see?

What we can do as a collective, we can’t do alone. When we see as one body, we don’t miss anything. Imagine if, when just one person is hurt or is suffering in your neighborhood, city, or country, the entire population becomes aware? As our digital connectivity brings us closer as humans, so should our nervous systems. Only then will we act as one body that can offer much-needed mutual repair.

The Role of Polyvagal Theory

Developed by Stephen Porges, PhD, the Polyvagal Theory outlines a theory of “how autonomic regulation shapes the body’s ongoing capacity to maintain stability, support health, and adapt to changing conditions.” In his work, he redefines stress as “a measurable state during which homeostatic functions are disrupted” and the process of neuroception as that which “functionally decodes and interprets the assumed goal of movements and sounds of inanimate and living objects.”

Trauma is one such disruption. When it disrupts the nervous system, the regulation needed, according to Porges, includes trauma-informed educational practices that emphasize rhythm, predictability, and relational safety. We can each “upgrade our nervous systems” by enhancing neuroplasticity, focusing on autonomic regulation, and engaging in practices that support vagal tone modulation.

When we are dysregulated, sitting with someone even briefly who can offer “relational presence” — listening quietly or engaging in sharing — can calm a nervous system. While there are dozens of apps available to measure our stress markers and provide soothing guidance, there’s no substitute for relating with another human being (as does a new app that I, Thomas, am offering, called “Attuned,” currently in Beta). In this app, a person who helps regulate, called an “Anchor,” is providing a nervous system to another as a service.

Just as we circulate financial currency, can we lend our nervous systems to one another, providing support even briefly when it’s most needed? What kind of full-scale economy of support and intelligence would this create for our world?

Just as individuals work on balancing the vagus nerve, entire communities can also. This form of practice is especially relevant during times of collective trauma: “At the community level, structural adversity − including racism, poverty, and violence − disrupts neuroception on a population scale, locking individuals and groups into chronic defensive states,” writes Porges.

Shaping Our Collective Nervous System: From Traumatized to Trauma-Integrating

When an individual or a collective is dysregulated, the roots of stress may point to past trauma. Here we outline a pathway for envisioning societal change that moves through four phases of working through trauma:

  • Traumatized

  • Trauma-informed

  • Trauma-sensitive

  • Trauma-integrative

A traumatized society suffers through the same symptoms an individual can experience; in this situation, there may be political and group dynamics that reflect unhealed wounds and negative consequences for citizens, as well as time-worn cycles of traumatization such as crime, substance abuse, mental health disorders, and violence. Often the trauma is rooted in the unseen, unhealed collective past. What we find is that the social ecosystem is hurt and fragmented, which tells us that the trauma “load” is much greater than the resources of the system. Just as an individual can feel separate from others because they’re carrying a high trauma load, so can a society.

In a trauma-informed society, the culture (through policy or educational shifts) is learning skills and protocols to prevent trauma and work through its aftermath. Leaders become early adopters of trauma awareness as they begin to anchor guidance into the social system, much like the way tending to acupuncture points helps heal the entire body. When leaders and citizens become trauma-aware, they learn to develop strategies to prevent re-traumatization, partnering with the early adopters to develop pockets of resilience for further learning.

As a society incorporates new practices and learning, they solidify these principles, becoming “trauma-sensitive.” Once trauma sensitivity is established, such as processes for working through discrimination, racism, sexism, gender violence, and other serious challenges, living a life that is based on trauma sensitivity becomes “the norm.” In these societies, emotional safety is a priority; people feel more empowered to speak up and report traumatic events; and more data is flowing within the social system.

Finally, a society that can be identified as “trauma-integrative” has intentionally moved through its trauma wounds through dedicated restoration processes. It embodies principles that value peace and a commitment to human dignity and rights. Resting on all the work of the former levels, the society now has shifted the balance to a greater presence of resources versus a trauma load. There is individual and collective maturation; decision-making is part of a natural flow. Diversity enriches the social field, without needing to enforce policies. There is profound healing; so much so that the collective intelligence – and nervous system – of the society is naturally revealed.

Activating our Collective Presence

In the current state of the world, we can point to many examples where collective actions or group behavior is not working towards the greater good. Can we turn our attention towards what it truly means to offer collective presence? Can we highlight models of progress where societies are succeeding? To begin, we first need to see clearly the "inner sculpture" of trauma that has been formed in our awareness through centuries of traumatic experiences, including wars, genocide, and other forms of oppression. When we restore our capacity to see from within ourselves as the collective, we restore the agency and power that is our birthright as humans without imagining there is a separate “world out there.”

We are that world. The collective nervous system is our power bank. Let’s reclaim it.

item.title: Why Are You Still Nice to Your Rude Adult Child?
item.description:
Parenting

Why Are You Still Nice to Your Rude Adult Child?

When generosity becomes a way to earn respect, parents pay an emotional price.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Tune in to what your kindness is trying to accomplish.
  • Separate your efforts to be understanding from accepting disrespect.
  • Let your kindness center on you as a person versus what you give.

Each week during parent coaching sessions, I hear something that goes like this: "Jimmy (age 31, fictitious name) constantly snaps at me, dismisses my feelings, and only reaches out when he needs something." Yet so many parents on the receiving end of similar rudeness still buy groceries, send money, rearrange their schedules, and carefully word each text. Later, these parents wonder: "Why am I doing so much for someone who treats me this way?"

The answer usually runs deeper than "I'm too nice." Look, I get it: You love your child, and you remember your happier moments. You hope your next thoughtful gesture will soften the tension and bring back the connection you miss. Wanting that connection isn't foolish. But when kindness becomes your strategy for preventing rejection, you can lose sight of your own needs.

A Brief Example of Susan and Veronica

Let's consider a woman I'll call Susan who contacted me last week about her adult daughter Veronica (fictitious name as well), who criticizes her and then asks her to cover another one of many bills. Susan told me she agrees, explaining, "If I say no, I panic that I'll lose the relationship." Afterward, as Susan unpacks it with me, she shares how she feels hurt and resentful. Of course, Veronica is oblivious to the emotional cost her mother is paying, which feels much higher to Susan than the money she doled out.

My book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!, guides parents on how to respond to the guilt, blame, and demanding behavior of struggling adult children while protecting both parties' dignity and mutual connection. Writing that book helped me reflect on the immense pain experienced by both parents and grown children whose relationships have gone awry because they lack calm, constructive conversations. Here are three ways to start buying back your emotional health without buying into a continued pattern of caving to your adult child when they are rude to you.

1. Tune In To What Your Kindness Is Trying To Accomplish

The next time your adult child sounds the "You need to help me" alarm, stop reaching for your "first-responder, kind parent-to-the-rescue uniform". I'm serious — enough already of leading a crisis-to-crisis-driven life with your adult child who is in lots of pain and taking it out on you. How is your adult child going to feel better about themself if you allow them to treat you like garbage?

To help you center yourself, before offering help or trying to solve a problem, reflect on: “Would I still want to do this if it earned me no gratitude, apology, or closeness?” What you don't want is to fall into the trap of "If I keep giving, perhaps my child will finally appreciate and be nicer to me." The trouble is that your adult child may see the favor simply as a favor—one that they believe they are entitled to ask for and receive. Meanwhile, you experience each ungrateful response as another rejection. So yes, give to your adult child when it fits your values and resources, and hit the pause button when fear is driving the decision.

2. Separate Understanding From Accepting Disrespect

Your adult child may feel overwhelmed, disappointed, or emotionally pained in one way or another. You can take those experiences seriously while setting limits on how you are treated. For example, how about saying something like, “I hear that you’re upset. I’m willing to talk about it calmly and constructively, but I’m going to pause this conversation if the insults continue.”

Most importantly, avoid turning setting this boundary into a courtroom argument about everything you have sacrificed. Long explanations can pull you back into defending your worth, so please know your value and stop doing that. You do not need your child to agree that a limit is fair before you honor it.

3. Let Kindness Center on You as a Person Versus What You Give

I remind parents I work with that they can send a birthday message without paying an overdue bill. They can listen but not remain on a call where they're being berated. Similarly, and this is a huge one, they can offer encouragement without taking over a problem their child can address. My advice is to start with one change you can sustain, such as fewer explanations/justifications, or a pause before agreeing, or a clear limit on financial help. Your child may dislike the change, but that reaction does not automatically mean you have done something wrong. It may mean you're interrupting an established pattern.

Final Thoughts

You do not have to become cold or otherwise emotionally distant to stop overfunctioning or overgiving. You can remain caring, available within reasonable limits, and open to connecting with your adult child when they are hurting.

But realize the question is no longer, “How can I be nice enough to make my child respect me?" Rather, the healthier question becomes, “How can I love my child without abandoning myself?”

item.title: Want to Indirectly Improve Relationships With Stepchildren?
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Want to Indirectly Improve Relationships With Stepchildren?

How stepparents can add value to the family.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • For most stepparents, positive bonds are built with stepchildren by being together and talking.
  • Sometimes, stepchildren resist a stepparent’s well-intentioned efforts to get to know them and become closer.
  • Perceiving that a stepparent enhanced family life and relationships can change stepchildren's feelings.
  • Stepparents can bond with distant stepchildren by building positive relationships with other family members.

We have been exploring how stepfamily members create satisfying relationships (see "First Steps for Stepparents," "Having Fun With Stepchildren," and other posts). Here, I continue this series, but instead of reviewing what stepparents can do directly with stepchildren to generate closer connections, I want to now explore an indirect approach to bonding with stepchildren: being a valuable addition to the family.

This advice is incredibly vague. What does “being a valuable addition to the family” mean? In this case, it means that a stepchild notices that the stepparent has made family life better. This is still unclear, so let’s drill down to see what the research says.

Most research findings about “what works” for stepparents trying to build good relationships with stepchildren focus on uncovering direct actions that stepparents do with stepchildren, either during one-on-one activities (e.g., playing games) or with other people around (e.g., going out to dinner as a family). For most stepparents and stepchildren, positive bonds are built this way; as with any new friendship, individuals seek common ground, enjoy doing things together, and talk/share a lot about their likes, interests, wants, needs, feelings, and thoughts, growing closer as the relationship develops. Direct approaches to bonding do not always work, however.

Sometimes, stepchildren resist a stepparent’s well-intentioned efforts to get to know them better and to become closer. There are lots of reasons for this, including loyalty to an absent parent, dislike of the stepparent for whatever reasons, personality clashes, and so on. Sometimes resistance is from only one stepchild, and sometimes all stepchildren in a family join in resisting their stepparents’ efforts to connect. When direct approaches to bonding with stepchildren are not working, there is still hope, because of an indirect pathway to stepparent-stepchild bonding: adding value to the family.

My research partners and I first encountered this in a study of the variability of stepparents’ relationships with stepchildren. In one pattern of how relationships developed, we found that some stepchildren drastically changed what they thought about a stepparent, even after months and years of sharing time in a household (see "Patterns of Stepchild-Stepparent Relationships" for more about this study). These changed perceptions led to big differences in how they interacted with their stepparent, and relationship quality greatly improved, going from distant or hostile feelings to warm and positive relationships. Perceptions began to change when stepchildren noticed that life in the household or the quality of other family interactions had improved because of the stepparent’s contributions.

Often, these stepchildren observed that their parent, the partner of the stepparent, was happier, less stressed, and seemed to enjoy life more. These stepchildren noticed how lovingly the stepparent interacted with their mom or dad; they observed how kind and respectful the stepparent was to their parent, and they could see that the stepparent had enriched the parent’s life. Perceiving that the stepparent enhanced the quality of life of their parent led to stepchildren feeling that they should be nicer to the stepparent as a way of indirectly repaying the stepparent’s kindness and support of the stepchild’s parent. These stepchildren reasoned, “I owe my stepfather because he has improved my mother’s life,” or “My dad seems much mellower and happier, so I need to give my stepmom a break.”

Other stepchildren changed the trajectories of relationships with stepparents after witnessing how warmly the stepparent interacted with their brothers and sisters, and after noting how positively their siblings felt about the stepparent. “If my brother and sister like him, and he likes them, maybe he is ok after all,” and “How can my stepmother be as bad as I think she is if my siblings have so much fun with her?” were typical comments we heard. Older stepchildren sometimes were less willing to try to get closer to the stepparent than their siblings, and it took time for them to “follow” their younger siblings in getting along better with the stepparent. Observing a stepparent helping a sibling with homework, paying for a school trip that they would have to miss before, or watching the stepparent and sibling having fun together were the kinds of positive interactions that led stepchildren to decide that the stepparent had added value to the family.

Noticing that the household was less emotionally stressful since the stepparent joined, perceiving that money was not as tight because of the stepparent’s added income, or seeing how much better other family members felt due to the stepparent’s support helped these initially resistant stepchildren conclude that the stepparent was a net addition to the family. Keep in mind that this indirect way of improving the step-bond usually does not happen overnight.

So, how can stepparents demonstrate they are adding value to the family? They can:

  • Be a good partner to the parent of the stepchild
  • Actively bond with stepchildren in tried and true ways (e.g., having fun together, working together, caregiving, etc.)
  • Be persistent in loving the parent and in trying to build friendships with stepchildren
  • Give resistant stepchildren some space, but provide them opportunities to see how you are adding to the well-being of all family members

Adding value to the family is easier said than done, perhaps. The good news is that stepparents can demonstrate adding value to the family by engaging in behaviors that researchers have found often lead to positive couple and stepparent-stepchild relationships. Also, parents and siblings can help resistant stepchildren notice a stepparent’s positive impacts and share their views about the stepparent’s contributions. The main takeaway message for stepparents is to hang in there in their efforts to build positive relationships with stepchildren — the benefits may well extend beyond the specific children with whom they are trying to bond.
